A close reading for the week

“this sceptered isle”

Richard II · Act 2, Scene 1

The most quoted praise of England in the language is the first half of an accusation: twenty lines of glory suspended in mid-sentence, waiting for a verb that arrives like a verdict.

GAUNTMethinks I am a prophet new inspired,1
And thus expiring do foretell of him:
His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last,
For violent fires soon burn out themselves;
Small showers last long, but sudden storms are short;

This royal throne of kings, this sceptered isle,2

  1. 1

    A dying man’s licence

    Elizabethans widely held that the dying spoke with prophetic truth, and Gaunt says so himself moments earlier: “the tongues of dying men / Enforce attention like deep harmony”. “New inspired” and “expiring” share a root: breath. His last breath is claimed as inspiration, which licenses what no subject could otherwise safely say about a king.

  2. 2

    “This… this… this”

    The speech runs on anaphora: the same demonstrative hammered at the head of phrase after phrase, more than a dozen times. Each “this” holds England up again at a slightly different angle: throne, earth, seat, fortress, breed, world, stone, plot, realm, nurse, womb. Grammatically, every one of them is a subject waiting for its verb, and the verb is withheld for twenty lines. The delay is part of the argument.
